title: Emotions and reactions
subtitle: crave, yearn, defuse, placate, over the moon
summary: Express strong desires, calm other people's anger, and describe pure happiness - from formal words like jubilant and rejoice to idioms like over the moon.

lesson.heading: Strong desires
lesson.text: To **crave** something, or **have a craving for** it, is to want it very strongly. To **thirst for** something, or **have a thirst for** it, is to feel very strongly that you want it. To **covet** something is to want to possess it very much.

examples.text: Pregnant women **crave** strange things like tuna and banana pizza!
Young children often seem to **have a thirst for** knowledge.
An Olympic gold medal is probably the most **coveted** sporting prize.
I'd give anything to own that motorbike of Nick's - I really **covet** it.

lesson.heading: Yearning for the impossible
lesson.text: If you **yearn to do** something, **yearn for** something or **have a yearning for** it, you want something you do not have and often can never have. **Yearn** carries sadness in a way that **crave** does not.

examples.text: Sometimes my cousin just **yearns** to be on her own with no family responsibilities.
I'm just **yearning** to return to my homeland again. But I don't think I ever will.
After the conflict he was **thirsting for** revenge - he was certainly not ready to forget it.

lesson.heading: Calming other people down
rows: make a dangerous or tense situation calmer
end a disagreement by acting in a friendly way towards both sides (formal)
end a disagreement by giving the other side what they demand (disapproving, formal)

lesson.heading: Using those verbs
lesson.text: You **defuse** a situation, you **placate** an angry person, and a third party **conciliates between** two sides. **Appease** is different: it suggests giving in weakly, so it is normally used disapprovingly.

examples.text: Lottie tried to **defuse the tension** by changing the subject.
Tim was very angry with his daughter and it took her a long time to **placate** him.
An independent advisor has been brought in to **conciliate between** the unions and the employer.
Although **appeasing** the enemy postponed the war for another year, it did not ultimately prevent it.

lesson.note: The useful adjective from placate is implacable: opinions or feelings that cannot be changed. There is no word placable.

lesson.heading: Formal words for great happiness
rows: feeling great pleasure because of a success (more formal than ecstatic)
be extremely happy (formal): everyone rejoiced at the news
expressing great happiness, especially at a victory (formal)
perfect happiness, often with utter or sheer; adjective blissful

lesson.heading: Bliss and blissfully
lesson.text: **Bliss** collocates with **utter** and **sheer**. The adverb **blissfully** goes especially with **happy**, **ignorant** and **unaware** - and in the last two it means happy precisely because you do not know something.

examples.text: Sarah was in an **exultant** mood after her great exam results.
There were **jubilant** shouts as the results of the referendum were announced.
Seven days on a beautiful island - **utter bliss**.
Fortunately, her parents were **blissfully ignorant** of what was going on.
They are **blissfully happy** even though they're poor.

lesson.heading: Informal ways of saying very happy
rows: full of the joys of spring
You look full of the joys of spring today. Why are you smiling all the time?
My daughter's just had a baby girl. We're thrilled to bits.
I feel on top of the world. It's great to have a job again.
I've been walking on air ever since I heard I got into drama school.
How did you feel when you scored the winning goal? I was over the moon!

lesson.text: Defuse a situation, placate a person: the object decides which verb you need.

exercises.prompt: I often find I ___ sweet things when I'm studying, but I try to resist!
exercises.explanation: To crave something is to want it very strongly.

exercises.prompt: Martha is very good at ___ difficult situations.
exercises.explanation: You defuse a situation - you placate a person.

exercises.prompt: Everyone is ___ to bits that Karim was so successful in the competition.
exercises.explanation: Thrilled to bits is a fixed informal expression meaning very happy.

exercises.prompt: If he has a tantrum, you mustn't try to ___ him. Don't give in!
exercises.explanation: To appease is to give the other side the advantage they are demanding - usually said with disapproval.

exercises.prompt: When Jess retires, there will be a lot of applicants for what must be the most ___ job in the company.
exercises.explanation: To covet something is to want to possess it very much; a coveted job is one many people want.

exercises.prompt: Fortunately, her parents were ___ ignorant of what was going on.
exercises.explanation: Blissfully collocates strongly with ignorant and unaware.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginnings and endings of these sentences.

pairs.right: on air since she got her promotion.
when they heard that the war had ended.
on top of the world since he got his PhD.
to bits when he won the medal.

exercises.prompt: Rowan says: 'I just want to learn more and more about science and history.' Rowan has a ___ for knowledge.
exercises.explanation: To have a thirst for something is to feel very strongly that you want it.

exercises.prompt: Katie says: 'I'm longing to return to my homeland, but I don't think I ever will.' Katie is ___ to go home.
exercises.explanation: To yearn for something is to want something you do not have and often can never have.

exercises.prompt: Ashley says: 'Calm down, there's no need to be so cross.' Ashley is trying to ___ someone.
exercises.explanation: To placate someone is to stop them feeling angry.

exercises.prompt: Lottie tried to ___ the tension by changing the subject.
exercises.explanation: To defuse a situation is to make a dangerous or tense situation calmer.

exercises.prompt: Seven days on a beautiful island - utter ___!
exercises.explanation: Bliss is perfect happiness; it collocates with utter and sheer.

exercises.prompt: How did you feel when you scored the winning goal? I was over the ___!
exercises.explanation: To be over the moon is an informal way of saying extremely happy.

exercises.prompt: Everyone ___ at the news of her recovery.
exercises.explanation: To rejoice is a formal way of saying to be extremely happy.

exercises.prompt: I cannot understand the ___ hatred that he still feels for his old rival.
exercises.hint: (the adjective from placate, with a negative prefix)
exercises.explanation: Implacable feelings or opinions cannot be changed. There is no word placable.

exercises.statement: If a politician talks about someone appeasing someone else, they are expressing approval.
exercises.explanation: No - appease and appeasement are normally used disapprovingly, suggesting weakness.

exercises.statement: Fans whose team has just won the World Cup would more naturally be called jubilant than blissful.
exercises.explanation: Correct - jubilant expresses great happiness especially at a victory.

exercises.statement: If you are trying to placate someone, they are probably over-excited rather than angry.
exercises.explanation: You placate someone who is angry. To calm a tense situation you defuse it.

exercises.prompt: Is each expression for happiness formal or informal?

items.text: full of the joys of spring

exercises.answer: I've been walking on air ever since I heard the news
exercises.explanation: To be walking (or floating) on air is an informal way of saying you are extremely happy.
